solution: The chapter states: "For this we established the Department of Atomic Energy and the Indian Atomic Energy Commission. The first Chairman ... was Dr Homi Bhabha. Even though electricity generation was the main purpose behind the programme, it also aimed at creating military capability." Electricity generation is the production/peaceful use of atomic energy, so (d) is the main objective; (a) military capacity is explicitly the secondary aim, and (b) nuclear tests (1974, 1998) and (c) non-proliferation are consequences/positions, not the founding objective.

The chapter repeatedly makes economic development the universal present-day goal: "Economic development is also an important national interest ... next only to defence", developing nations formed regional organisations because "They felt that economic development was more important", and in the second stage "the priority no longer remained to political and military relations ... Efforts began to be made to increase the rate of economic growth." Atomic development and nuclear tests are pursued by only a few countries, and a security system is treated as national interest rather than as the shared objective of all nations now.

Non-alignment is presented as the defining feature of India's foreign policy: "Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru contributed the policy of non-alignment to India's foreign policy", and in the First Stage summary "India adopted the policy of non-alignment in the context of the cold war ... Due to the policy of non-alignment, India could get aid from both the super powers." Caveat: the chapter also contains the near-verbatim sentence "India's nuclear policy is an important part of India's foreign policy", which is a close rival to the 'nuclear development' option — but that option names a capability the chapter describes as one element rather than an aspect of the policy itself, and interdependence is a feature of the international system (Ch.1), not of India's policy.

The chapter says "India conducted her first nuclear tests in 1974", and the History companion chapter names the site: "India successfully carried out an underground test of an atomic device at Pokharan in Rajasthan in 1974." Shriharikota and Thumba are space-launch sites and Jaitapur a nuclear power project site; none is mentioned as a test site in the chapter.
